# Twelve-Tone Serial Matrix Composition (TTSMC) (Method 065)

### **Source**
Twelve-tone serialism is the foundational 20th-century atonal composition method, first codified by Josef Matthias Hauer ("law of the twelve tones", 1919) and independently by Arnold Schoenberg (1921–1923), who described it as a "method of composing with twelve tones which are related only with one another". The canonical theoretical treatment is **Babbitt, M. (1960), "Twelve-Tone Invariants as Compositional Determinants," *Musical Quarterly* 46(2)** — which formalizes the row as an ordered 12-tuple of pitch classes under the transformations of transposition, inversion, and retrograde, and proves which properties (invariants) survive each operation. The complete group-theoretic formulation is **Perle, G. (1977), *Twelve-Tone Tonality*** (and *Serial Composition and Atonality*, 1962), which derives the 48-form set-complex (12 transpositions × {P, R, I, RI}) and the combinatoriality/invariance theory; **Babbitt, M. (1955), "Some Aspects of Twelve-Tone Composition," *Score and I.M.A. Magazine* 12** adds the combinatoriality doctrine (hexachordal aggregates completing the chromatic). The algorithmic lineage runs through **Hiller, L. & Isaacson, L. (1959), *Experimental Music* (the ILLIAC Suite)** — the first computer composition, which used rule-based serial procedures — and **Wuorinen, C. (1979), *Simple Composition***, the standard practical manual. In the Musicom catalog, TTSMC fills the *permutational determinism* gap: 001 Skeleton-First and 013 Inversion/Retrograde apply geometric transforms to motifs, 025 Xenakis Sieve builds scales by congruence, 056 SCCC enforces species counterpoint — but none treats the *pitch-class aggregate itself* (all 12 chromatic tones, each exactly once) as the generative object. TTSMC is the Rules-Based, aggregate-driven counterpart to the stochastic pitch generators (002 Markov, 023 Tendency Masking, 053 LFC) and the atonal foil to the tonal-gravity methods (006 Cadence, 014 Negative Harmony, 050 OTVL).

### **Description**
Twelve-Tone Serial Matrix Composition (TTSMC) generates music from a single ordered 12-tuple of pitch classes — the **tone row** $P = (p_0, p_1, \dots, p_{11})$, a permutation of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ — and its 48 derived forms. The four basic operations generate the set-complex:

- **Prime** $P$: the row as written.
- **Retrograde** $R$: $P$ read backwards, $R_i = p_{11-i}$.
- **Inversion** $I$: each pitch-class interval direction reversed about the first pitch class, $I_i = (2p_0 - p_i) \bmod 12$.
- **Retrograde-Inversion** $RI$: $I$ read backwards.

Transposing any of the four by $t$ semitones gives $P_t, R_t, I_t, RI_t$ — 48 forms total. The **12×12 serial matrix** (the "magic square") tabulates all 48 forms: row 0 is $P$, column 0 is $I$, each row is a transposition of $P$, each column a transposition of $I$, the anti-diagonals are $R$ forms, and the main diagonals are $RI$ forms. Composition = *scheduling* row forms across the UnitMatrix: each section (column) is assigned one or more row forms, each voice (row) reads a form (or a partition of one), and the aggregate property — all 12 pitch classes sounding exactly once per row statement — replaces tonal function as the structural glue. Because every pitch class carries equal weight, the music is atonal by construction; large-scale form is articulated not by key areas but by *row-form regions* (e.g., exposition on $P_0$/$I_6$, development on $R_0$/$RI_6$), *invariants* (pitch-class sets preserved under transformation, used as pivots between forms), and *combinatorial pairs* (two hexachords from different forms that together complete the aggregate). **Complexity**: generating a row form is $\mathcal{O}(12)$; filling a $V \times S$ UnitMatrix with $F$ row statements is $\mathcal{O}(F \cdot 12)$ — trivially linear.

### **Musical Elements Framework**
- **PITCH**: The row *is* the pitch material. Every melody is a row form (or a derived partition of one) read left-to-right; every simultaneity is a segment of a form read vertically (partitioning). Because each form contains all 12 pitch classes exactly once, pitch repetition is forbidden within a statement — the aggregate is the unit of pitch syntax. Registral freedom (any octave) and rhythmic freedom (any duration) are the composer's only degrees of freedom within a strict statement; this is exactly the "topography" Schoenberg exploited (row order fixed, register/rhythm free).
- **RHYTHM**: The row fixes pitch *order* only, so rhythm is a free parameter — but serial practice derives it too: rhythmic series (durations as ordered sets, per Babbitt's time-point system), or mapping row order numbers to onset offsets within a bar. In TTSMC, each section assigns a rhythmic profile (Euclidean groove 012, isorhythmic talea 032, or a serialized duration row) to its row statement; the aggregate pitch order rides on top of the rhythmic grid.
- **HARMONY**: Vertical sonorities are *partitions* of a row form — adjacent segments of the row stacked as chords. Partitioning a form into trichords/tetrachords yields the harmony; because the row is a permutation of the chromatic, any full partition sums to the aggregate. Combinatoriality is the harmonic engine: two forms whose first hexachords are complementary (e.g., $P_0$ and $I_6$) can be sounded simultaneously to produce complete 12-note aggregates every hexachord — the serial replacement for consonant chord progression. Invariant pitch-class sets (shared segments between forms) act as pivot chords at form boundaries.
- **STRUCTURE**: Macro-form = row-form architecture. Sections are assigned forms from the matrix (e.g., A = $P_0$, B = $I_6$, A′ = $R_0$), so form is expressed as a network of transformations rather than key relationships. The 48-form matrix is the structural palette; choosing a path through it (which form per section, which transposition level) *is* composing the form. Combinatorial pairs define large sections (hexachordal aggregate blocks); invariant pivots smooth the joins.
- **TEXTURE**: Texture = row distribution across voices. A single form partitioned across $V$ voices gives homophonic aggregate chords; $V$ voices each reading a different form simultaneously gives polyphonic aggregate counterpoint (Webern's multidimensional set presentations); derived rows (trichord/tetrachord generators) give imitative texture where every voice states the same small cell in transformation. Voice count is free — the row is distributed, not duplicated.

### **UnitMatrix Integration (Voices and Sections)**
- **Rows (Voices)**: Each voice $v$ reads a row form (or a partition of one) over a section. Voice 1 = $P_0$ melody; Voice 2 = $I_6$ counter-melody (combinatorial partner); Voice 3 = vertical partition of $P_0$ (chord tones); Voice 4 = $R_0$ in augmentation (rhythmic series). Voices may share a form (partitioning = homophony) or read different forms (aggregate counterpoint); the aggregate property is enforced *per voice* (each voice completes the chromatic before repeating a pitch class).
- **Columns (Sections)**: Each section $s$ is assigned a row form $F_s$ from the 48-form matrix (e.g., A = $P_0$, B = $I_6$, A′ = $R_0$, C = $RI_6$). The section's chord function is replaced by its *row-form region*; combinatorial pairs ($P_0$/$I_6$) define section-scale aggregate blocks. Section joins use invariant pitch-class pivots (shared segments between $F_s$ and $F_{s+1}$) for smooth transitions.
- **Cells**: Each cell $U_{v,s}$ contains:
  - `{PITCH}`: The pitch-class segment of form $F_s$ assigned to voice $v$ in section $s$, octave-registered to the voice's range.
  - `{RHYTHM}`: Onset offsets from the section's rhythmic profile (Euclidean/talea/serialized duration row) applied to the row segment.
  - `{HARMONY}`: The partition scheme (trichord/tetrachord/hexachord) that stacks the row segment into the cell's vertical sonority.
  - `{TEXTURE}`: Row distribution mode — partitioned (homophonic), multi-form (polyphonic), or derived (imitative).
- **Mapping Flow**:
  1. Choose a prime row $P$ (a permutation of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$); build the 12×12 serial matrix (all 48 forms).
  2. Assign a row form $F_s$ to each section; choose combinatorial pairs and invariant pivots at the joins.
  3. Partition each form across the voices (or assign per-voice forms) and apply the section's rhythmic profile.
  4. Octave-register pitch classes to each voice's range; quantize onsets to the tick grid.
  5. Fill UnitMatrix cells $U_{v,s}$ with the resulting MusicUnits; validate zero-drift and export via the musicom engine.

### **Technical Mechanics**
The serial matrix is computed by fixing $P$ (row 0) and deriving column 0 as the inversion about $p_0$: $I_0 = (2p_0 - p_i) \bmod 12$. Row $t$ is then $P$ transposed by the interval from $p_0$ to $I_0[t]$; equivalently the full matrix is

$$M[t][i] = \big(p_i + (I_0[t] - p_0)\big) \bmod 12$$

so every row is a transposition of $P$ and every column a transposition of $I_0$. The 48 forms are read off the matrix: row $t$ = $P_t$, column $t$ = $I_t$, row $t$ reversed = $R_t$, column $t$ reversed = $RI_t$. **Invariants**: a pitch-class set (segment) that maps to itself (or its complement) under a transformation is a pivot — e.g., if $P$'s first trichord equals $I_6$'s first trichord, that trichord is invariant and can bridge the two forms. **Combinatoriality**: $P$ and $I_6$ are hexachordally combinatorial iff the first hexachord of $P$ and the first hexachord of $I_6$ are disjoint and together cover $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ (Babbitt's aggregate doctrine). **Derivation**: a row is *derived* if all its trichords/tetrachords are transformations of a single generator cell (Webern's Op. 24 row is derived from a single trichord) — this is the serial analogue of motivic unity. **Complexity**: matrix build $\mathcal{O}(144)$; each row statement $\mathcal{O}(12)$; total fill $\mathcal{O}(F \cdot 12)$ for $F$ statements — linear, deterministic, seedable.

### **Implementation Requirements (Python / NumPy)**
```python
import numpy as np

def serial_matrix(P):
    """P: length-12 permutation of Z_12. Returns 12x12 matrix M[t][i]."""
    P = np.array(P) % 12
    p0 = P[0]
    I0 = (2 * p0 - P) % 12          # inversion about p0 (column 0)
    M = np.zeros((12, 12), dtype=int)
    for t in range(12):
        M[t] = (P + (I0[t] - p0)) % 12   # row t = P transposed by I0[t]-p0
    return M

def row_forms(M):
    """All 48 forms: P_t, R_t, I_t, RI_t."""
    forms = {}
    for t in range(12):
        P_t  = M[t].tolist()
        I_t  = M[:, t].tolist()
        forms[f"P{t}"]  = P_t
        forms[f"R{t}"]  = P_t[::-1]
        forms[f"I{t}"]  = I_t
        forms[f"RI{t}"] = I_t[::-1]
    return forms

def partition(form, scheme):
    """Split a 12-tone form into segments (e.g. [3,3,3,3] or [4,4,4])."""
    out, i = [], 0
    for k in scheme:
        out.append(form[i:i+k]); i += k
    return out

def is_combinatorial(P, Q):
    """Hexachordal combinatoriality: first hexachords disjoint, union = Z_12."""
    return set(P[:6]).isdisjoint(set(Q[:6])) and set(P[:6]) | set(Q[:6]) == set(range(12))
```

- **Tooling**: NumPy for the matrix arithmetic; musicom engine for UnitMatrix fill and zero-drift MIDI export. No training, no corpus, no randomness required (though row choice and rhythmic profiles can be seeded/stochastic).
- **Parameter set**: prime row $P$ (a permutation of $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$), per-section form assignment $F_s$, partition scheme per voice, rhythmic profile per section, octave registration per voice.

### **Pitfalls**
1. **Pitch-class vs. pitch confusion**: The row is a sequence of *pitch classes* (0–11), not pitches. Naive implementations emit the same octave for every note, producing a cramped, unmusical line. Fix: octave-register each pitch class to the voice's range (e.g., nearest MIDI octave to a register center), and allow registral freedom within a statement.
2. **Aggregate violation (pitch repetition)**: Repeating a pitch class before the row completes breaks the aggregate and the atonal premise. Fix: enforce a per-voice "used pitch-class" set that resets only at the end of each row statement; validate each voice's statement completes $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$.
3. **Staccato / sparse texture**: Strict serial pointillism (one note per row position, wide gaps) produces the sparse, gap-filled texture the user rejected (the 011/032 failure mode). Fix: per the Method Hybridization rule, add a continuous fill layer — sustained aggregate chords (partitioned row held as pads), DPSM 026 phase-shifted row arpeggios, or a walking bass that cycles the row in steady eighths.
4. **Monotonous row recycling**: Repeating the same form at the same transposition level flattens the piece into one 12-note loop. Fix: rotate through the 48-form matrix (different forms/transpositions per section), use combinatorial pairs for contrast, and exploit invariants as pivots so form changes are audible.
5. **Atonal drift (no tonal anchor)**: Pure aggregate equality gives zero tonal gravity — the music can feel unmoored. Fix: if a tonal center is desired, derive the row from a scale (e.g., a row whose hexachords outline two complementary modes), or pair TTSMC with 022 MCWS quantization to pull aggregate pitches toward a HOME region (hybrid atonal/tonal).
6. **Rhythmic monotony**: If every row statement uses the same rhythmic profile, the aggregate order becomes predictable. Fix: serialize rhythm too (duration rows, Babbitt time-point sets), or vary the rhythmic profile per section (012 Euclidean / 032 talea / 026 DPSM).
7. **Parallel octaves in partitioning**: Stacking the same pitch class in two octaves across voices (partition overlap) creates hollow parallel octaves. Fix: ensure partition segments are disjoint pitch-class sets per simultaneity, and register voices in distinct ranges.
8. **Off-grid drift**: Serialized onset offsets (order number → time) can land between ticks. Fix: quantize onset offsets to the tick grid, and run `composer.validate()` before export (same zero-drift gate as every method).

### **Comparison With Related Methods**
- **001 Skeleton-First**: structural grid from DNA seeds; TTSMC's skeleton is the 48-form matrix — the form *is* the structure, no separate grid needed.
- **013 Inversion/Retrograde**: applies P/R/I transforms to motifs; TTSMC is the full 12-tone generalization — the transforms act on the complete chromatic aggregate, not a local motif.
- **025 Xenakis Sieve**: builds scales by modular congruence; TTSMC builds pitch material by permutation — both are modular arithmetic over $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$, but sieve = subset selection, serial = ordering.
- **056 SCCC**: rules-based counterpoint against a cantus firmus; TTSMC is the atonal rules-based counterpart — the row replaces the cantus firmus and the mode, aggregate completion replaces consonance rules.
- **002 Markov / 053 LFC**: stochastic pitch generation with tonal gravity; TTSMC is deterministic, aggregate-exact, and atonal — the rules-based foil to stochastic pitch methods.

- Babbitt, M. (1955). "Some Aspects of Twelve-Tone Composition." *Score and I.M.A. Magazine* 12: 53–61.

# Generative Theory of Tonal Music Hierarchical Composition (GTTM-HC) (Method 066)

### **Source**
The Generative Theory of Tonal Music (GTTM) is the foundational cognitive-musicology account of how an experienced listener unconsciously parses tonal music, developed by music theorist **Fred Lerdahl** and linguist **Ray Jackendoff** in their 1983 book *A Generative Theory of Tonal Music* (MIT Press). It was directly inspired by Leonard Bernstein's 1973 Charles Eliot Norton Lectures at Harvard, where Bernstein called for a "musical grammar" in the spirit of Noam Chomsky's transformational-generative linguistics — GTTM is that grammar. The theory posits four interacting hierarchical systems: **Grouping Structure** (motives → phrases → periods → sections), **Metrical Structure** (hierarchically alternating strong/weak beats), **Time-Span Reduction** (a tree of "heads" — the most structurally important event in each time-span), and **Prolongational Reduction** (a tree encoding tensing/relaxing patterns via three branch types: strong prolongation, weak prolongation, progression). Each system is defined by three rule classes: **well-formedness rules** (WFRs, what structures are legal), **preference rules** (PRs, which legal structure a listener actually hears), and **transformational rules** (mapping distorted surfaces back to well-formed descriptions). The algorithmic lineage is the Hamanaka–Hirata–Tojo line: **ATTA** (Automatic Time-span Tree Analyzer, ISMIR 2005), **FATTA** (Full Automatic Time-span Tree Analyzer, ICMC 2007), and the ExGTTM analyzer (Hamanaka, Hirata & Tojo 2006, *Journal of New Music Research* 35(4)); the tension dimension is quantified by **Lerdahl & Krumhansl (2007), "Modeling Tonal Tension," *Music Perception* 24(4)**, building on Lerdahl's *Tonal Pitch Space* (2001). In the Musicom catalog, GTTM-HC fills the *music-theoretic hierarchy* gap: 034 PCFG does Chomskyan rewrite with free, probabilistic rules; 056 SCCC does species counterpoint against a cantus firmus; 001 Skeleton-First drafts a structural grid — but none models the *listener's* hierarchical hearing (grouping + meter + reduction + tension) as the generative object. GTTM-HC is the Rules-Based, tonal-hierarchy counterpart to the stochastic pitch generators (002/053) and the deterministic foil to the free-grammar 034 PCFG.

### **Description**
GTTM is canonically an *analysis* theory (score → four trees). GTTM-HC inverts it into a *generation* method: compose the deep prolongational structure first (a Schenkerian-style skeleton — tonic triad with a descending structural line), then recursively **elaborate** each branch with diminutions (passing tones, neighbor tones, arpeggiations) governed by the well-formedness rules, place the resulting events on the metrical grid, and read off the grouping structure from the elaboration tree. The four systems are generated in dependency order — meter constrains grouping, grouping + meter constrain time-span reduction, and time-span reduction constrains prolongational reduction — so the whole composition is one self-consistent hierarchical description, exactly the object GTTM's rules adjudicate. The prolongational tree's three branch types carry the harmonic/tension semantics: **strong prolongation** (open node) = same event sustained/embellished without harmonic motion (relaxation), **weak prolongation** (filled node) = neighbor/arpeggiation motion within the same harmony (mild tension), **progression** (no node) = actual harmonic movement (tension). The tension curve over the piece is computed by the Lerdahl–Krumhansl model $T(y) = T_{loc}(y) + T_{diss}(y) + T_{hier}(y)$ — pitch-space distance from the tonic plus sensory dissonance plus hierarchical branching penalty — and this curve *is* the macro-form's HOME/LIFT/TENSE/TURN trajectory. Because every event is placed by a rule (never sampled from a distribution), the method is fully deterministic and seedable; the only stochastic degrees of freedom are optional (which preference rule wins a tie, which diminution pattern is chosen at equal strength).

### **Musical Elements Framework**
- **PITCH**: Pitch material comes from the recursive prolongational elaboration of the deep structure. The structural line (e.g., scale degrees $\hat{3} \to \hat{2} \to \hat{1}$ over I–V–I) supplies the "heads" — the most structurally important pitches at each time-span level. Diminutions fill between heads: passing tones (stepwise motion between two heads a third apart), neighbor tones (step away and back to the same head), and arpeggiations (chord-tone skips within the governing harmony). Register is free (octave placement of heads), but the pitch-class content of every event is constrained by the current harmony and the stepwise-motion preference (PRPR — prolongational preference rules favor small intervals).
- **RHYTHM**: The metrical structure is the rhythmic engine: a multi-level grid of strong/weak beats (e.g., bar > half-note > quarter > eighth). Heads are placed on strong beats at their time-span level; elaborations occupy weaker subdivisions. Rhythmic density is controlled by how deep the elaboration recursion runs — deeper recursion = more diminutions = denser surface rhythm. The metrical well-formedness rules (MWFRs) guarantee every level is a regular alternation of strong/weak, so the output is always grid-locked and groove-compatible.
- **HARMONY**: Harmony is the prolongational tree itself. A strong-prolongation branch means the harmony is *prolonged* (no chord change); a progression branch means harmonic movement (e.g., I → V → I). The deep structure fixes the tonal plan (tonic prolongation, dominant preparation, cadence), and each elaboration preserves the harmonic function of its parent branch. Tension-relaxation is read directly off the tree: progression branches raise $T_{hier}$, strong prolongations lower it — so the harmony *is* the tension architecture, not a separate chord loop.
- **STRUCTURE**: Macro-form = the top levels of the grouping + prolongational trees. The piece is one root group; its children are the large sections (A/B/A′); each section's prolongational branch type determines its function (progression-heavy = TENSE/LIFT development, strong-prolongation-heavy = HOME statement). Because the tree is built top-down, form is explicit and hierarchical — a genuine rondo/ABA emerges when the root's children are parallel groups (GPR6 parallelism), exactly the macro-form other methods (051 SGLM, 052 QWC) achieve only via graph topology.
- **TEXTURE**: Texture = how the elaboration tree is distributed across voices. A single tree read monophonically gives a melody; the same tree partitioned across voices gives homophonic chordal texture (heads stacked vertically); multiple trees (one per voice) sharing the same metrical/grouping structure give polyphonic counterpoint where each voice is an independent elaboration of the same deep structure. Texture density = number of active elaboration branches at the surface level.

### **UnitMatrix Integration (Voices and Sections)**
- **Rows (Voices)**: Each voice $v$ is either (a) a partition of the single prolongational tree (homophonic — voice 1 carries the structural line, voices 2–4 carry the vertical stacks of each head), or (b) its own elaboration tree derived from the same deep structure but with a different diminution pattern (polyphonic — independent counter-melodies that share the tonal plan). All voices share the metrical and grouping structures, so they are grid-synchronized and phrase-aligned by construction.
- **Columns (Sections)**: Each section $s$ is a child of the root group — a top-level branch of the grouping tree. Its prolongational branch type sets the section's chord function: strong prolongation = HOME, progression = TENSE/TURN, weak prolongation = LIFT. The section's tension curve (from the Lerdahl–Krumhansl model) is the macro-form trajectory across columns.
- **Cells**: Each cell $U_{v,s}$ contains:
  - `{PITCH}`: The head pitch of the cell's time-span (the most structurally important event in that span), plus its diminutions (passing/neighbor/arpeggiation) elaborated to the cell's recursion depth.
  - `{RHYTHM}`: Onset offsets from the metrical grid — heads on strong beats, elaborations on weak subdivisions.
  - `{HARMONY}`: The prolongational branch type of the cell's node (strong/weak/progression), which fixes the chord function.
  - `{TEXTURE}`: Elaboration density — number of active diminution branches at the surface within the cell.
- **Mapping Flow**:
  1. Define the deep structure: tonic triad + structural line (e.g., $\hat{3}\hat{2}\hat{1}$ over I–V–I), one node per section.
  2. Build the metrical grid (multi-level strong/weak beats) and the grouping tree (recursive binary segmentation via GPR2/GPR3/GPR5/GPR6).
  3. Build the time-span tree: assign each time-span its head (most metrically strong + harmonically stable event).
  4. Build the prolongational tree: connect heads with branch types (strong/weak/progression) per the tonal plan.
  5. Elaborate: recursively expand each branch with diminutions to the target recursion depth; place events on the metrical grid.
  6. Distribute the tree across voices (partition or per-voice trees); fill UnitMatrix cells $U_{v,s}$; validate zero-drift and export via the musicom engine.

### **Technical Mechanics**
The four systems and their dependency order:

1. **Metrical structure**: a grid $M$ of levels $L_0 \succ L_1 \succ \dots \succ L_k$ (bar > beat > subdivision), each a regular strong/weak alternation (MWFRs). Beats at level $L_i$ are a subset of beats at $L_{i+1}$.
2. **Grouping structure**: a tree over the event sequence. Preference rules score each inter-onset gap as a boundary candidate: GPR2 (proximity — larger IOI = boundary), GPR3 (change — register/dynamics/articulation/length change = boundary), GPR5 (symmetry — prefer equal halves), GPR6 (parallelism — parallel segments form parallel groups). Boundaries are chosen greedily top-down from the highest-scoring gaps, subject to GWFRs (contiguous, exhaustive, non-overlapping groups).
3. **Time-span reduction**: for each group, the head is the event that is (a) on the strongest beat and (b) most harmonically stable (chord root/fifth over passing dissonance). Recursing gives the time-span tree.
4. **Prolongational reduction**: connect heads into a tree with branch types — **strong prolongation** (open node: same event, no harmonic motion), **weak prolongation** (filled node: motion within the same harmony), **progression** (no node: harmonic movement). The tree must satisfy PRWFRs (e.g., no crossing branches).

**Tension** (Lerdahl–Krumhansl 2007, simplified): for a chord/event $y$,

$$T(y) = T_{loc}(y) + T_{diss}(y) + T_{hier}(y)$$

where $T_{loc}(y) = \delta(y \to tonic)$ is the Tonal Pitch Space distance (circle-of-fifths steps + chord-space steps) from $y$ to the tonic, $T_{diss}(y)$ is the sensory dissonance of the chord, and $T_{hier}(y)$ is the hierarchical branching penalty (progression > weak prolongation > strong prolongation = 0). The sequence of $T(y)$ over heads is the piece's tension curve.

**Generation (inverse)**: start from the deep structure (root prolongational tree), then repeatedly apply elaboration operators — *passing* (insert a stepwise event between two heads a third apart), *neighbor* (insert a step above/below a head and return), *arpeggiation* (insert chord tones between heads) — until the surface reaches the metrical grid resolution. Each elaboration preserves the parent's branch type and harmonic function, so the final tree is well-formed by construction.

**Complexity**: grouping via boundary scoring + top-down segmentation is $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ (sort boundary strengths); time-span head selection $\mathcal{O}(N)$; prolongational tree build $\mathcal{O}(N)$; elaboration $\mathcal{O}(N)$ in number of surface events. Total $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ — linear-ish, deterministic, seedable.

### **Implementation Requirements (Python / NumPy)**
```python
import numpy as np
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

# --- Metrical grid: multi-level strong/weak beats ---------------------------
def metrical_grid(n_bars, beats_per_bar, levels):
    """levels: subdivisions per beat at each metrical level, e.g. [1, 2, 4]."""
    grid = []
    for bar in range(n_bars):
        for beat in range(beats_per_bar):
            for sub in range(levels[-1]):
                strength = sum(1 for lv in levels if sub % lv == 0)
                grid.append({"bar": bar, "beat": beat, "sub": sub,
                             "strength": strength, "tick": (bar * beats_per_bar * levels[-1] + beat * levels[-1] + sub)})
    return grid

# --- Grouping: preference-rule boundary scoring -----------------------------
def boundary_scores(events):
    """GPR2 proximity + GPR3 change. events: list of (tick, pitch, vel, dur)."""
    scores = []
    for i in range(1, len(events)):
        ioi_prev = events[i][0] - events[i-1][0]
        ioi_next = events[i+1][0] - events[i][0] if i+1 < len(events) else ioi_prev
        prox = (ioi_prev > ioi_next) + (ioi_prev > 0)  # GPR2: larger gap = boundary
        change = (abs(events[i][1] - events[i-1][1]) > 6) + \
                 (abs(events[i][2] - events[i-1][2]) > 20)  # GPR3: register/dynamics
        scores.append((prox + change, i))
    return sorted(scores, reverse=True)

def grouping_tree(events, scores, max_groups=4):
    """Greedy top-down binary segmentation subject to GWFRs (contiguous, exhaustive)."""
    bounds = [0, len(events)]
    for strength, i in scores:
        if len(bounds) - 1 >= max_groups:
            break
        if i not in bounds and i > 0 and i < len(events):
            bounds.append(i)
    bounds.sort()
    return [events[a:b] for a, b in zip(bounds[:-1], bounds[1:])]

# --- Prolongational tree + tension -----------------------------------------
@dataclass
class PNode:
    pitch: int                 # head pitch (MIDI)
    branch: str = "progression"  # strong | weak | progression
    children: list = field(default_factory=list)

def tonal_tension(pitch, tonic, chord_roots):
    """Simplified Lerdahl-Krumhansl: pitch-space distance + branching penalty."""
    pc = pitch % 12
    fifths = min((pc - tonic) % 12, (tonic - pc) % 12)  # circle-of-fifths steps
    t_loc = fifths + (0 if pc in chord_roots else 2)      # chord-space distance
    return t_loc

def elaborate(node, depth, scale, chord_tones, rng):
    """Recursive prolongational expansion: passing / neighbor / arpeggiation."""
    if depth == 0:
        return [node.pitch]
    out = []
    for child in node.children:
        out.extend(elaborate(child, depth - 1, scale, chord_tones, rng))
        if node.children.index(child) < len(node.children) - 1:
            nxt = node.children[node.children.index(child) + 1].pitch
            gap = nxt - child.pitch
            if abs(gap) == 2:                     # passing tone
                out.append(child.pitch + gap // 2)
            elif abs(gap) > 2:                    # arpeggiation
                mid = chord_tones[rng.integers(0, len(chord_tones))]
                out.append(mid)
            else:                                  # neighbor tone
                out.append(child.pitch + (1 if rng.random() < 0.5 else -1))
    return out

# ... add_voice / add_section ...
# for each section s (a root child), for each voice v (tree partition):
#   events = elaborate(section_tree[v], depth=recursion_depth, ...)
#   place heads on strong beats, elaborations on weak beats (metrical grid)
#   composer.fill_voice_section(voice, section, create_note_unit(pitch, dur, start_tick))
# ok, msg = composer.validate()   # MUST be True before to_midi
```
- **Tooling**: NumPy for grid/score arrays; musicom engine for UnitMatrix fill and zero-drift MIDI export. No training, no corpus — pure rule evaluation.
- **Parameter set**: deep structure (tonic, structural line, tonal plan), metrical levels, recursion depth (surface density), preference-rule weights (GPR2/3/5/6), diminution pattern (passing/neighbor/arpeggiation mix), voice distribution mode (partition vs. per-voice trees).

### **Pitfalls**
1. **Analysis/generation direction confusion**: GTTM is canonically an *analysis* theory — naive implementations try to "analyze then resynthesize," which just reproduces the input. Fix: generate top-down from the deep structure (prolongational skeleton first, then elaborate); the rules are used as *construction* constraints, not as a parser.
2. **Sparse / staccato surface**: If recursion depth is too shallow or heads are placed on every strong beat with no diminutions, the output is the 011/032 sparse-texture failure mode (gap-filled, non-flowing). Fix: per the Method Hybridization rule, elaborate to a depth that fills weak subdivisions (passing/neighbor/arpeggiation), or add a continuous fill layer (sustained head-chord pads, 026 DPSM phase-shifted arpeggios of the structural line).
3. **Branch-type / harmony mismatch**: Marking a branch "strong prolongation" while the surface harmony actually changes produces a tree that contradicts the music (PRWFR violation). Fix: enforce that strong prolongation = no chord change, weak prolongation = motion within one harmony, progression = chord change; validate the tree against the tonal plan before elaboration.
4. **Metrical rigidity**: Placing every head on beat 1 and every elaboration on exact subdivisions yields a stiff, quantized feel. Fix: allow heads on the strongest beat *within their time-span* (not always bar downbeat), and let weak-beat elaborations carry syncopation via the metrical grid's sub-levels.
5. **Preference-rule ties (ambiguity)**: GPR2/GPR3/GPR5/GPR6 frequently conflict or tie, and a naive greedy picker produces unstable groupings. Fix: weight the PRs (e.g., parallelism GPR6 > proximity GPR2 > change GPR3), and break residual ties deterministically (earliest boundary wins) for reproducibility.
6. **Voice independence collapse**: Partitioning one tree across voices can stack the same head pitch in parallel octaves (hollow texture, cf. TTSMC pitfall 7). Fix: register voices in distinct ranges, and for polyphonic mode give each voice its own elaboration tree (different diminution patterns) so lines are independent.
7. **Tension monotony**: If every section uses the same branch-type sequence, the tension curve is flat. Fix: vary the prolongational plan per section (progression-heavy development vs. strong-prolongation statement), and use the Lerdahl–Krumhansl $T(y)$ curve to verify the HOME/LIFT/TENSE/TURN arc before export.
8. **Off-grid drift**: Diminutions placed at fractional beats land between ticks. Fix: quantize all onset offsets to the metrical grid's tick resolution, and run `composer.validate()` before export (same zero-drift gate as every method).

### **Comparison With Related Methods**
- **034 PCFG Recursion**: Chomskyan rewrite with free, weighted rules; GTTM-HC is the music-theoretic counterpart — the rewrite rules are the well-formedness/preference rules of tonal hearing, and the non-terminals are prolongational branch types, not abstract symbols.
- **001 Skeleton-First**: drafts a structural grid from DNA seeds; GTTM-HC's skeleton is the deep prolongational structure (tonic triad + structural line) — the skeleton *is* the tonal plan, and the grid (meter) is generated, not assumed.
- **056 SCCC**: species counterpoint against a cantus firmus; GTTM-HC is the hierarchical reduction counterpart — the structural line replaces the cantus firmus, and prolongational branching replaces species dissonance rules.
- **051 SGLM / 052 QWC**: derive macro-form from graph spectra/topology; GTTM-HC derives form from the grouping + prolongational trees — the tree *is* the form, no graph needed.
- **002 Markov / 053 LFC**: stochastic pitch generation with weak tonal gravity; GTTM-HC is deterministic with strict tonal gravity (every event anchored to the tonic via the reduction tree) — the rules-based foil to stochastic pitch methods.

### **References**
- Lerdahl, F., & Jackendoff, R. (1983). *A Generative Theory of Tonal Music*. MIT Press.
- Lerdahl, F. (2001). *Tonal Pitch Space*. Oxford University Press.
- Lerdahl, F., & Krumhansl, C. L. (2007). "Modeling Tonal Tension." *Music Perception* 24(4): 329–366.
- Lerdahl, F. (2009). "Genesis and Architecture of the GTTM Project." *Music Perception* 26: 187–194.
- Hamanaka, M., Hirata, K., & Tojo, S. (2006). "Implementing a Generative Theory of Tonal Music." *Journal of New Music Research* 35(4): 249–277.
- Hamanaka, M., Hirata, K., & Tojo, S. (2005). "ATTA: Automatic Time-span Tree Analyzer based on Extended GTTM." *ISMIR 2005*: 358–365.
- Hamanaka, M., Hirata, K., & Tojo, S. (2007). "FATTA: Full Automatic Time-span Tree Analyzer." *ICMC 2007*: 153–156.
- Hirata, K., Tojo, S., & Hamanaka, M. (2007). "Techniques for Implementing the Generative Theory of Tonal Music." *ISMIR 2007 Tutorial*.
- Bernstein, L. (1976). *The Unanswered Question: Six Talks at Harvard*. Harvard University Press. (The 1973 Norton Lectures that motivated GTTM.)
# CORDIS-ANIMA Modular Mass-Interaction Network Synthesis (MMINS) (Method SP-052)

### **Source**
CORDIS-ANIMA is the mass-interaction physical modeling formalism created by **Claude Cadoz, Annie Luciani, and Jean-Loup Florens at the ACROE laboratory in Grenoble, France**, beginning with Cadoz's doctoral work (*"Synthèse sonore par simulation de mécanismes vibratoires,"* INPG Grenoble, 1979) and first published in English as **Cadoz, C., Luciani, A., and Florens, J.-L. (1984), "Responsive Input Devices and Sound Synthesis by Stimulation of Instrumental Mechanisms: The CORDIS System," *Computer Music Journal* 8(3), pp. 60–73**. The canonical formalism paper is **Cadoz, C., Luciani, A., and Florens, J.-L. (1993), "CORDIS-ANIMA: A Modeling and Simulation System for Sound and Image Synthesis: The General Formalism," *Computer Music Journal* 17(1), pp. 19–29** (DOI 10.2307/3680567). The module vocabulary and the "instrumental universe" concept are consolidated in **Florens, J.-L. and Cadoz, C. (1991), "The Physical Model: Modeling and Simulating the Instrumental Universe," in *Representations of Musical Signals*, MIT Press**. The compositional environment built on the formalism is **GENESIS** (ACROE), described for musical applications in **Cadoz, C., Castagné, N., and Tache, O. (2011), "Sound synthesis and musical composition with the physical modeling formalism Cordis-Anima," *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 130(4), 2365** (DOI 10.1121/1.3654476). Hybridization with digital waveguides is treated in **Kontogeorgakopoulos, A. and Cadoz, C. (2008), "Interfacing Digital Waveguide with CORDIS ANIMA networks," *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 123(5)** (DOI 10.1121/1.2934998), which characterizes CORDIS-ANIMA as "a highly modular lumped physical modeling and simulation system based on the mass-interaction paradigm." In the Musicom catalog, MMINS fills the *modular lumped-graph* gap: SP-011/SP-023/SP-024/SP-033 are delay-line waveguides (fixed 1D/2D topology), SP-040 is a PDE grid, SP-042 is a fixed-object eigenmode bank, and SP-018 (Scanned Synthesis) uses a mass-spring chain only as a *wavetable source*. CORDIS-ANIMA instead makes the *arbitrary network of point masses and links* the instrument itself, with nonlinear contact/friction links and the audio signal read directly from a mass point's displacement.

### **Description**
CORDIS-ANIMA models a sounding object as a **network of lumped physical modules** — point masses with inertia (the *CORDIS* material layer) connected by force-generating links (the *ANIMA* interaction layer). The vocabulary is tiny: **MAT** (mass point), **SOL** (fixed ground point), **LIA** (viscoelastic link = spring + damper), **RES** (pure resistive damper), **FRO** (nonlinear friction, for bowing/stick-slip), **BUT** (butée — unilateral stop/contact, for impacts and rattling). The network is simulated **at audio sample rate**: each sample, every link computes an interaction force from the current positions/velocities of its two endpoints, and every mass integrates the net force via a centered finite-difference discretization of Newton's second law. The **displacement of one or more mass points is the audio signal** — there is no separate oscillator/render stage; the simulation *is* the synthesis. Because the topology is an arbitrary graph, the same formalism builds a plucked string (chain of masses), a drumhead (2D grid), a bowed string (chain + FRO link), a rattling shaker (masses + BUT stops), or a whole coupled orchestra. The formalism also unifies *gesture and instrument*: the excitation is itself a network (a mass driven by a force source) that strikes, bows, or plucks the instrument network — the "instrumental universe." **Complexity**: $\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{masses}} + N_{\text{links}})$ per sample — linear in network size, real-time for networks of hundreds of modules.

### **Technical Mechanics**

**1. Material point (MAT) — inertia.** Newton's second law $F = M\,\ddot{x}$ discretized with the centered (leapfrog/Verlet) finite-difference scheme at sample period $T = 1/f_s$:

$$x(n+1) = 2\,x(n) - x(n-1) + \frac{T^2}{M}\,F(n)$$

The mass point carries only two state variables ($x(n)$, $x(n-1)$); velocity is reconstructed as $v(n) = \big(x(n) - x(n-1)\big)/T$.

**2. Ground point (SOL).** A fixed reference of infinite mass: $x(n) = 0$ for all $n$. It absorbs force without moving — anchoring a LIA to SOL yields a simple harmonic oscillator.

**3. Viscoelastic link (LIA) — spring + damper.** Connecting masses $i$ and $j$ with stiffness $K$ and damping $Z$:

$$F_{ij} = -K\,(x_i - x_j) - Z\,(v_i - v_j)$$

The force is applied to $i$ and, with opposite sign, to $j$ (Newton's third law). A single MAT anchored to SOL by a LIA is a damped harmonic oscillator with natural frequency $f_0 = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{K/M}$.

**4. Resistive link (RES) — pure damper.** $F_{ij} = -Z\,(v_i - v_j)$; dissipates energy without storing it.

**5. Nonlinear links.** **FRO** (friction) implements stick-slip bowing: when relative velocity is near zero it holds with static force $F_s$; once slipping, it applies kinetic force $F_d < F_s$ against the motion. **BUT** (butée) is a unilateral stop: a one-sided spring active only past a limit displacement, $F = -K\,\max(x_i - x_j - x_{\text{lim}},\,0)$, producing impacts, fret buzz, and rattling.

**6. Simulation loop (per audio sample).**
1. **Force pass**: zero all mass forces; add external excitations $F_{\text{ext}}$ (pluck impulse, bow drive, noise); for each link compute $F_{ij}$ and accumulate into both endpoints with opposite signs.
2. **Integration pass**: for each MAT, $x(n+1) = 2x(n) - x(n-1) + \tfrac{T^2}{M}\sum F$.
3. **Output**: $y(n) = x_k(n)$ (displacement of the output mass) or a weighted sum over several output masses.

**7. Stability.** The scheme is conditionally stable; the stiffest mode must be resolved: $\omega_0 = \sqrt{K/M}$ requires $\omega_0 T \ll 2$ (equivalently $T \ll 2\sqrt{M/K}$). CORDIS-ANIMA runs at 44.1 kHz precisely so the time step is the audio period; stiff links (high $K$, low $M$) are the constraint.

**8. Modal structure = timbre.** A chain of $N$ masses with LIA links has $N$ eigenmodes; a 2D grid has $N_x \cdot N_y$; the network's stiffness matrix (assembled from the link graph) determines the modal spectrum. Topology *is* timbre: chain = string-like harmonic series with dispersion, grid = membrane with inharmonic partials, tree = branching resonator. Damping $Z$ sets per-mode decay; nonlinear links inject broadband energy (bow noise, impact transients).

**Complexity**: per sample — one force evaluation per link plus one integration per mass, $\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{masses}} + N_{\text{links}})$. Vectorized as sparse matrix-vector products: the force pass is $F = -K_{\text{sparse}}\,x - Z_{\text{sparse}}\,v$, the integration pass is a per-mass update — trivially parallel across masses.

### **Musical Elements Framework**
- **PITCH**: Set by the network's eigenmodes. A MAT–LIA–SOL oscillator has $f_0 = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{K/M}$; retuning = changing $K$ or $M$. Chains and grids give inharmonic partial series (dispersion), so pitch is the *fundamental of the modal spectrum*, not a single oscillator frequency. Per-voice pitch = the voice network's lowest mode; chord tones = multiple oscillators or one multi-mode network tuned to the chord.
- **RHYTHM**: The excitation schedule. Pluck impulses at tick-grid onsets (grid-locked); FRO bowing produces stick-slip periodicity (the Helmholtz motion's natural period — continuous, self-oscillating rhythm); BUT contacts produce impact transients at collision instants. The network imposes no grid of its own — it follows the onset schedule of the driving force exactly.
- **HARMONY**: The modal spectrum *is* the harmonic content. A single oscillator = pure partial; a chain = harmonic series with inharmonic stretch; a grid = dense inharmonic cluster. Coupling several oscillators (one per chord tone) through LIA links yields sympathetic resonance — the harmonic equivalent of a chord with shared overtones. Nonlinear links generate intermodulation (sum/difference partials) between modes.
- **STRUCTURE**: Macro-form via topology and parameter trajectories per section. Section A = plucked chain (bright, short decay); section B = bowed chain (sustained, FRO); section C = membrane grid (dense pad). Adding/removing links at section joins switches the instrument; slow automation of $K$, $Z$, or excitation force gives continuous timbral morphs (the physical counterpart of SP-041 wavetable morphing).
- **TEXTURE**: Network density (masses + links), damping $Z$ (decay time), and nonlinearity (FRO/BUT) are the texture knobs. Sparse networks = thin, resonant; dense grids = thick, noisy; high $Z$ = dry/percussive; low $Z$ = long ringing; FRO/BUT add grit, bow noise, and rattling. The "instrumental universe" lets texture itself be a network — a rain of small BUT-contact masses for granular rattle.

### **UnitMatrix Integration (Voices and Sections)**
- **Rows (Voices)**: Each voice $v$ is an independent CORDIS-ANIMA network (or a sub-network of a shared instrument). Voice 1 (lead) = plucked string chain (MAT chain + LIA, anchored to SOL); Voice 2 (bass) = bowed string (chain + FRO link driven by a moving ground); Voice 3 (pad) = membrane grid (2D MAT grid + LIA, high $Z$); Voice 4 (percussion) = rattle (masses + BUT stops, noise-driven). Each row renders to a mono buffer, then summed or spatialized (SP-021/SP-034/SP-043).
- **Columns (Sections)**: Each section $s$ supplies (a) the network topology or parameter set ($K$, $M$, $Z$, link graph), (b) the excitation pattern (impulse schedule, bow force trajectory, noise injection), and (c) the output mass selection. Section joins = topology switch (discrete instrument change) or parameter crossfade (continuous morph).
- **Cells** $U_{v,s}$:
  - `{PITCH}`: $K$/$M$ values (or retune factor) — the cell's fundamental/modal tuning.
  - `{RHYTHM}`: Excitation impulse onsets and bow-force envelope — the cell's attack schedule.
  - `{HARMONY}`: Modal spectrum — number of masses in the chain/grid, link coupling (the cell's overtone structure).
  - `{TEXTURE}`: Damping $Z$, FRO/BUT presence and thresholds, network density — the cell's decay, grit, and density.
- **Mapping Flow**:
  1. Compose and fill the UnitMatrix; validate zero-drift; export MIDI via the musicom engine (symbolic layer).
  2. Build one CORDIS-ANIMA network per voice; map each cell's `{PITCH}` to $K$/$M$ retuning, `{RHYTHM}` to excitation impulses (velocity → force amplitude), `{TEXTURE}` to $Z$/nonlinearity.
  3. Simulate each network at audio rate, driven by the cell's excitation schedule; read output mass displacement as the voice buffer.
  4. Sum voices; post-process (SP-007 EQ, SP-008 DRC, SP-009/SP-032 reverb); export or spatialize (SP-021/SP-034/SP-043).

### **Implementation Requirements (Python / NumPy)**
```python
import numpy as np

class MassInteractionNetwork:
    """CORDIS-ANIMA style mass-interaction network (SP-052 MMINS)."""
    def __init__(self, fs=44100):
        self.fs = fs
        self.T = 1.0 / fs
        self.masses = {}   # id -> dict(M, x, x_prev, F)
        self.links = []    # (type, i, j, params)

    def add_mass(self, m_id, M, x0=0.0):
        self.masses[m_id] = dict(M=M, x=x0, x_prev=x0, F=0.0)

    def add_ground(self, g_id):
        self.masses[g_id] = dict(M=np.inf, x=0.0, x_prev=0.0, F=0.0)  # SOL

    def add_lia(self, i, j, K, Z):
        self.links.append(('LIA', i, j, dict(K=K, Z=Z)))

    def add_res(self, i, j, Z):
        self.links.append(('RES', i, j, dict(Z=Z)))

    def add_fro(self, i, j, Fs, Fd):
        self.links.append(('FRO', i, j, dict(Fs=Fs, Fd=Fd)))

    def add_but(self, i, j, K, x_lim):
        self.links.append(('BUT', i, j, dict(K=K, x_lim=x_lim)))

    def step(self, excitations):
        """One audio sample. excitations: {mass_id: external force}."""
        T = self.T
        for m in self.masses.values():
            m['F'] = 0.0
        for m_id, f in excitations.items():
            self.masses[m_id]['F'] += f
        # 1) force pass
        for typ, i, j, p in self.links:
            mi, mj = self.masses[i], self.masses[j]
            xi, xj = mi['x'], mj['x']
            vi = (mi['x'] - mi['x_prev']) / T
            vj = (mj['x'] - mj['x_prev']) / T
            if typ == 'LIA':
                F = -p['K'] * (xi - xj) - p['Z'] * (vi - vj)
            elif typ == 'RES':
                F = -p['Z'] * (vi - vj)
            elif typ == 'FRO':                      # Coulomb stick-slip (bowing)
                dv = vi - vj
                F = -np.sign(dv) * p['Fd'] if abs(dv) > 1e-6 else -np.clip(p['Fs'], -p['Fs'], p['Fs'])
            elif typ == 'BUT':                      # unilateral stop (impact)
                F = -p['K'] * max(xi - xj - p['x_lim'], 0.0)
            mi['F'] += F
            mj['F'] -= F                            # action-reaction
        # 2) integration pass
        for m in self.masses.values():
            if np.isinf(m['M']):
                continue                            # ground stays fixed
            x_new = 2.0 * m['x'] - m['x_prev'] + (T * T / m['M']) * m['F']
            m['x_prev'], m['x'] = m['x'], x_new
        return self.masses

# --- Example: plucked string = chain of N masses with LIA links ---
net = MassInteractionNetwork(fs=44100)
N = 32
for k in range(N):
    net.add_mass(k, M=0.001)
net.add_ground('g')
for k in range(N - 1):
    net.add_lia(k, k + 1, K=2000.0, Z=0.5)
net.add_lia(N - 1, 'g', K=2000.0, Z=0.5)           # anchor to ground

# render: pluck mass 0 once, read displacement of mass N//2
buf = []
for n in range(44100):                              # 1 second
    exc = {0: 100.0} if n == 0 else {}               # impulse at t=0
    m = net.step(exc)
    buf.append(m[N // 2]['x'])
audio = np.array(buf)
```
- **Tooling**: NumPy for the per-sample loop; vectorize by assembling the sparse stiffness/damping matrices ($F = -K_{\text{sparse}}x - Z_{\text{sparse}}v$) and updating all masses in one array operation. Compile with Numba/Cython for real-time. The musicom engine handles UnitMatrix fill and zero-drift MIDI export upstream; MMINS consumes the symbolic layer downstream (pitch → $K$/$M$ retune, velocity → excitation force).
- **Parameter set**: per-voice network topology (masses, links, module types), $M$/$K$/$Z$ per module, FRO/BUT thresholds, excitation schedule, output mass selection, sample rate.

### **Pitfalls**
1. **Instability (exploding network)**: The centered-difference integrator blows up if the stiffest mode is under-resolved ($\omega_0 T \ge 2$). Fix: enforce $T \ll 2\sqrt{M/K}$ — clamp $K$, raise $M$, or oversample; validate the network's maximum eigenvalue before rendering.
2. **DC drift / undamped ringing**: A lossless network (no $Z$) integrates numerical error into a slowly growing DC offset or never decays. Fix: add a small $Z$ to every LIA (even $10^{-4}$ stabilizes); high-pass the output.
3. **Sparse / staccato output**: Impulse-only excitation with fast decay gives plucky, gap-filled textures — the 011/032 failure mode. Fix: per the Method Hybridization rule, add a continuous fill layer — sustained FRO bowing (moving ground), high-$Z$ membrane pads, or noise-driven rattle networks.
4. **Monophonic sine monotony**: A single MAT–LIA–SOL oscillator is a pure damped sine. Fix: use chains/grids for inharmonic spectra, couple multiple oscillators (sympathetic resonance), or add FRO/BUT for broadband energy.
5. **Pitch sharpness from discretization**: $f_0 = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{K/M}$ is exact only in continuous time; the discrete scheme shifts pitch slightly sharp. Fix: pre-warp $K$ using the discrete dispersion relation $\omega_d = \tfrac{2}{T}\arcsin(\omega_a T/2)$, or measure the rendered fundamental and retune.
6. **Nonlinear link chatter**: Hard BUT/FRO contacts can chatter at Nyquist (limit-cycle buzz). Fix: regularize the contact law (smooth the max/sign transitions), add a small compliance, or oversample the nonlinear links.
7. **Per-sample Python loop too slow**: A network of hundreds of modules at 44.1 kHz in pure Python is too slow for long renders. Fix: vectorize the force/integration passes with sparse matrices, or compile (Numba/Cython); the DSP is $\mathcal{O}(N_{\text{masses}} + N_{\text{links}})$ per sample — real-time in compiled code.

### **Comparison With Related Methods**
| Method | Domain | Topology | Nonlinearity | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Modal Plate/Bar (SP-003) | Frequency domain (modes) | Fixed object | None | $O(N_{\text{modes}})$ |
| Karplus-Strong (SP-011) | Delay line | 1D string | None | $O(N)$ |
| Scanned Synthesis (SP-018) | Mass-spring chain as wavetable | 1D chain | None | $O(N)$ |
| FDTD (SP-040) | PDE on spatial grid | 2D/3D grid | Optional | $O(N_{\text{grid}})$ |
| Modal Bank MBED (SP-042) | Eigenmode resonators | Fixed object | None | $O(N_{\text{modes}})$ |
| **MMINS (SP-052)** | **Lumped mass-interaction graph** | **Arbitrary graph** | **FRO/BUT contact + friction** | $O(N_{\text{masses}} + N_{\text{links}})$ |

### **References**
- Cadoz, C., Luciani, A., and Florens, J.-L. (1993). "CORDIS-ANIMA: A Modeling and Simulation System for Sound and Image Synthesis: The General Formalism." *Computer Music Journal* 17(1), pp. 19–29. DOI 10.2307/3680567.
- Cadoz, C., Luciani, A., and Florens, J.-L. (1984). "Responsive Input Devices and Sound Synthesis by Stimulation of Instrumental Mechanisms: The CORDIS System." *Computer Music Journal* 8(3), pp. 60–73. DOI 10.2307/3679813.
- Florens, J.-L., and Cadoz, C. (1991). "The Physical Model: Modeling and Simulating the Instrumental Universe." In *Representations of Musical Signals*, MIT Press, pp. 227–268.
- Cadoz, C., Castagné, N., and Tache, O. (2011). "Sound synthesis and musical composition with the physical modeling formalism Cordis-Anima." *Journal of the Acoustical Society of America* 130(4), 2365. DOI 10.1121/1.3654476.
- Kontogeorgakopoulos, A., and Cadoz, C. (2008). "Interfacing Digital Waveguide with CORDIS ANIMA networks." *Journal of the Acoustical Society of America* 123(5), 3902. DOI 10.1121/1.2934998.
- Cadoz, C. (1979). *Synthèse sonore par simulation de mécanismes vibratoires.* Doctoral thesis, INPG, Grenoble, France.
- Florens, J.-L., Cadoz, C., and Luciani, A. (1997). "A MARACA Modelisation and Simulation through the CORDIS-ANIMA Formalism." *Proc. International Symposium on Musical Acoustics (ISMA)*, Edinburgh.
# Vector Base Amplitude Panning (VBAP) (Method SP-053)

### **Source**
VBAP was introduced by **Ville Pulkki** at the Helsinki University of Technology in the canonical paper **Pulkki, V. (1997), "Virtual Sound Source Positioning Using Vector Base Amplitude Panning," *Journal of the Audio Engineering Society* 45(6), pp. 456–466**. The perceptual validity of the method (localization quality, phantom-source width, and the tangent-law/sine-law relationships it instantiates) is established in the two-part follow-up **Pulkki, V. (2001), "Localization of Amplitude-Panned Virtual Sources II: Two- and Three-Dimensional Panning," *J. Audio Eng. Soc.* 49(9), pp. 753–767** and **Pulkki, V. (2000), "Generic Panning Tools for MAX/MSP," *Proc. ICMC***. A consolidated textbook treatment appears in **Pulkki, V. and Karjalainen, M. (2015), *Communication Acoustics*, Wiley**, and the method is positioned as the *object-based* counterpart to *scene-based* ambisonics in **Zotter, F. and Frank, M. (2019), *Ambisonics*, Springer**. In the Musicom catalog, VBAP fills the object-based gap: SP-021 is headphones-only binaural HRTF, SP-034 is scene-based HOA (render-system agnostic, speaker layout fixed only at decode), and SP-043 is physical WFS wavefront reconstruction. VBAP works directly on *arbitrary discrete loudspeaker arrays* with amplitude gains alone — no filters, no delays per source — making it the default panning layer between a mono voice render and a spatial mix.

### **Description**
VBAP is the canonical **object-based amplitude panning** algorithm. A virtual source is placed at an arbitrary direction by feeding its signal, at computed gains, to the smallest set of loudspeakers whose position *vectors* enclose that direction: **two adjacent speakers in 2D** (pair-wise panning on a horizontal ring) or **three speakers forming a triangle in 3D** (triplet panning on a full sphere). The speaker direction vectors form a *vector base*; the source direction is represented as a positive linear combination of the base vectors, and the combination coefficients *are* the panning gains. Because a unit-length source vector is used, the gains are non-negative and sum (in the constant-power normalization) with $\sum_i g_i^2 = 1$, keeping perceived loudness constant as the source glides around the array. Full-sphere coverage is obtained by **triangulating the loudspeaker set** into a mesh of triangles (3D) or segments (2D) and selecting, per source position, whichever simplex contains the source direction. Gains are *continuous* across shared edges, so a moving source morphs smoothly between neighboring speaker triplets. Unlike HRTF binaural (SP-021) — which costs one convolution pair per source and is sweet-spot limited — VBAP uses a single scalar gain per active speaker per sample, so it scales to dozens of simultaneous sources at near-zero cost. It is amplitude-only: no interaural time difference is synthesized, so elevation and distance are conveyed only through level (and optionally per-speaker delay/distance attenuation), with HRTF fold-down layered on top when headphone reproduction is needed. **Complexity**: $\mathcal{O}(T)$ one-time precompute (invert each triangle matrix), then $\mathcal{O}(1)$ per source per sample.

### **Technical Mechanics**

**1. Direction vectors.** Each loudspeaker $k$ is represented by a unit vector $\mathbf{l}_k$ pointing from the listener toward the speaker, and the virtual source by a unit vector $\mathbf{p}$ at azimuth $\theta$ and elevation $\phi$:

$$\mathbf{l}_k = \big(\cos\theta_k \cos\phi_k,\ \sin\theta_k \cos\phi_k,\ \sin\phi_k\big)^\top,\qquad \mathbf{p} = \big(\cos\theta \cos\phi,\ \sin\theta \cos\phi,\ \sin\phi\big)^\top$$

**2. 2D pair-wise panning.** With two adjacent speakers $\mathbf{l}_1, \mathbf{l}_2$ and a source between them, require the source vector to be a positive linear combination of the base:

$$\mathbf{p} = g_1 \mathbf{l}_1 + g_2 \mathbf{l}_2
\;\Longrightarrow\;
[\,g_1\ g_2\,] = \mathbf{p}^\top\,\big[\mathbf{l}_1\ \mathbf{l}_2\big]^{-1}$$

In azimuth-only form with $\theta_1 < \theta < \theta_2$ this reduces to the **sine law**:

$$g_1 = \frac{\sin(\theta_2 - \theta)}{\sin(\theta_2 - \theta_1)},\qquad
g_2 = \frac{\sin(\theta - \theta_1)}{\sin(\theta_2 - \theta_1)}$$

**3. 3D triplet panning.** With three speakers forming a (non-degenerate) triangle containing $\mathbf{p}$, build the $3{\times}3$ matrix whose columns are the base vectors and solve the $3{\times}3$ linear system:

$$\mathbf{p} = g_1 \mathbf{l}_1 + g_2 \mathbf{l}_2 + g_3 \mathbf{l}_3 = L_{123}\,\mathbf{g}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{p}^\top\, L_{123}^{-1},\qquad L_{123} = \big[\mathbf{l}_1\ \mathbf{l}_2\ \mathbf{l}_3\big]$$

where $\mathbf{g} = [g_1, g_2, g_3]$. The triangle is the correct one iff all three gains are non-negative.

**4. Constant-power normalization.** Pulkki's equalized VBAP scales the gains so that the *sum of squares* is unity:

$$\mathbf{g}' = \frac{\mathbf{g}}{\|\mathbf{g}\|}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
g_1^{\prime 2} + g_2^{\prime 2} + g_3^{\prime 2} = 1$$

This yields the perceptually flat (constant-power) phantom image: a source dead-center of a stereo pair gets $g_1 = g_2 = 1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707$ per channel. It is exactly the equal-power form of the classic **tangent law** $\tan\theta / \tan\theta_0 = (g_1 - g_2)/(g_1 + g_2)$, and it is what prevents the center-collapse loudness bump of constant-amplitude ($\sum g_i = 1$) panning.

**5. Mesh / triangulation.** The full loudspeaker array is triangulated once (Delaunay triangulation of the speaker vectors). For each source, the containing simplex is found by testing barycentric coordinates (all $\ge 0$) or by a point-in-triangle test; the corresponding pre-inverted matrix $L_{123}^{-1}$ is then applied. The **inverse is precomputed per triangle** so that a running source costs one matrix–vector product. Gains are continuous across shared triangle edges (changing the *set* of active speakers occurs exactly at an edge, where the shared two gains coincide), so source motion morphs without clicks.

**6. Hybrid panning (elevation with horizontal ring).** To pan to an elevated source using only a horizontal ring plus a few high speakers, VBAP synthesizes a **virtual loudspeaker**: two real horizontal speakers at gains $g_1^\prime, g_2^\prime$ are combined to act as a single speaker at azimuth $\theta_s$ and direction $\mathbf{p}_{v} \parallel g_1^\prime \mathbf{l}_1 + g_2^\prime \mathbf{l}_2$. The elevated source is then panned in 2D between $\mathbf{p}_v$ and a high real speaker. This gives smooth vertical motion without a full sphere of speakers.

**7. Distance.** Optional per-source depth: scale all gains by a distance term and delay each speaker feed by the propagation lag,

$$g_i^{\text{(d)}} = g_i \cdot \frac{d_{\text{ref}}}{d},\qquad \Delta t_i = \frac{d_i}{c}$$

For true headphone/virtual reproduction, the summed speaker channels are post-folded through per-speaker HRTFs (SP-021) or an ambisonic decoder (SP-034).

**Complexity**: precompute $\mathcal{O}(T)$ (invert $T$ triangle $3{\times}3$ matrices); per-sample per-source $\mathcal{O}(1)$ (one $3$-vector solve + normalization, amortized over a block of samples since trajectories are smooth). Memory $\mathcal{O}(K + T)$ for $K$ speakers, $T$ triangles.

### **Implementation Requirements (Python / NumPy / SciPy)**
```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial import Delaunay

def speaker_vec(az, el):
    """azimuth/elevation in radians -> unit direction vector (x=front, y=left, z=up)."""
    ce = np.cos(el)
    return np.array([np.cos(az) * ce, np.sin(az) * ce, np.sin(el)])

class VBAP:
    """Vector Base Amplitude Panning (SP-053)."""
    def __init__(self, speaker_az, speaker_el):
        self.ls = np.array([speaker_vec(a, e)
                            for a, e in zip(speaker_az, speaker_el)])      # (K,3)
        if self.ls.shape[0] < 3:
            self.tri, self.inv = None, None                                # 2D ring handled separately below
        else:
            self.tri = Delaunay(self.ls)                                   # simplex = (T,3) idx arrays
            self.inv = [np.linalg.inv(self.ls[sim]) for sim in self.tri.simplices]

    def gains(self, az, el):
        p = speaker_vec(az, el)
        if self.tri is None:                                               # 2D fallback: adjacent pair
            a = np.arctan2(self.ls[:, 1], self.ls[:, 0]) % (2 * np.pi)
            pa = np.arctan2(p[1], p[0]) % (2 * np.pi)
            idx = np.argsort(a)
            b, w = np.empty(2), np.empty(2)
            for a1, a2 in zip(idx, np.roll(idx, -1)):
                lo, hi = a[a1], a[a2]
                if hi < lo: hi += 2 * np.pi
                pa2 = pa if pa >= lo else pa + 2 * np.pi
                if lo <= pa2 <= hi:
                    b, w = [a1, a2], [np.sin(hi - pa2), np.sin(pa2 - lo)]
                    w /= np.linalg.norm(w)                                 # constant power
                    return b, w
            return None, np.zeros(2)
        for sim, inv in zip(self.tri.simplices, self.inv):
            g = p @ inv                                                   # p^T L^{-1}
            if np.all(g > -1e-9):                                         # inside this triangle
                g = np.clip(g, 0.0, None)
                n = np.linalg.norm(g)
                if n > 1e-12:
                    g = g / n                                             # constant power
                return sim, g
        return None, np.zeros(3)

    def render(self, source_sig, az, el):
        """Pan a mono buffer along scalar azimuth/elevation trajectories."""
        K = len(self.ls)
        out = np.zeros((K, len(source_sig)))
        for n in range(len(source_sig)):
            sim, g = self.gains(az[n], el[n])
            if sim is not None:
                np.add.at(out, sim, g * source_sig[n])
        return out   # shape (K, N): per-loudspeaker signals
```
**Tooling**: NumPy/SciPy as above; vectorize by precomputing per-triangle gains for a whole trajectory block and advanced-indexing the output; JIT the per-sample loop with Numba for hundreds of sources. The musicom engine supplies the symbolic UnitMatrix + zero-drift MIDI upstream; each voice is rendered mono by its synthesis engine (e.g. SP-029 subtractive, SP-016 granular), then VBAP places it per its `{PITCH/RHYTHM/HARMONY/TEXTURE}`-derived trajectory. **Parameter set**: loudspeaker layout (azimuth/elevation vectors), triangle mesh, per-source azimuth/elevation/distance automation, normalization mode, hybrid virtual-loudspeaker pairs, HRTF fold-down flag.

### **Musical Elements Framework**
- **PITCH**: VBAP is amplitude-only, so pitch content is untouched — but a register↔space map is a powerful orchestration device: bass = front-center (stable anchor, maximal phantom focus), mid leads = slight off-center, high shimmer/pads = wide or rear. Spatial placement *separates* simultaneous pitch strata that spectrally overlap, functioning as a "spatial EQ."
- **RHYTHM**: The panning layer is continuous-time and grid-free; rhythmic character comes from *when* the symbolic layer decides to move. Onset-locked jumps (position steps exactly at note-on events), tempo-synced LFO pan (sine/square at beat divisions), or step automations per bar turn spatial motion into a groove element. VBAP itself never quantizes; it faithfully follows the trajectory keyframes handed to it.
- **HARMONY**: Chord voices can be spread across azimuth so each pitch-class occupies a distinct direction — *spatial harmony*. An equiangular triad (three voices at 120° spacing in a triplet) gives maximal voice separation without changing the chord; narrowing the spread blends the chord into a single phantom image. The tangent law governs this separation aurally — it is the harmonic "voicing width" knob of the spatial domain.
- **STRUCTURE**: Spatial macro-form. Each section is a *spatial scene*: verse = narrow front suite (sources bundled, slow drift), chorus = full-width horizontal spread (voices explode to ±60°), bridge = elevated/rear surround (hybrid top speakers), cadence = all sources collapse to center (structural closure in space). Section joins are either hard scene cuts or continuous morphs (trajectory interpolation), the spatial analogue of a register plan or a harmonic cadence.
- **TEXTURE**: Spatial density — the number of simultaneous sources, their angular spread, distance distribution, and motion speed — is the textural dimension VBAP controls directly. A sparse front trio reads as intimate and dry; a full-sphere densely moving cloud reads as immersive and thick. Distance attenuation + per-source reverb send (SP-032) layer depth into the texture.

### **UnitMatrix Integration (Voices and Sections)**
- **Rows (Voices)**: Each voice $v$ is an independent virtual source with its own spatial trajectory envelope `az[v](t), el[v](t), d[v](t)`. Voice 1 (lead) = front-center with slow wobble; Voice 2 (bass) = front-center anchor (stationary); Voices 3–4 (harmony/backing) = wide ±40° pair; Voice 5 (pad) = rear elevated diffuse spray (several correlated sub-sources). Voice independence in the pitch/harmony domain is mirrored by spatial independence — overlapping registers stay intelligible because they do not share a direction.
- **Columns (Sections)**: Each section $s$ supplies a *spatial scene*: base azimuth band, spread width, elevation band, movement speed, and distance profile. Section A = narrow front, Section B = full-width spread, Section C = rear/surround — a spatial macro-form that parallels the harmonic/register macro-form already encoded per column.
- **Cells** $U_{v,s}$:
  - `{PITCH}`: register → spatial band (bass to center, highs to wide/rear); octave transposition keeps its cell-level spatial meaning.
  - `{RHYTHM}`: pan-move keyframe timing — onset-locked jumps, LFO rate division, step-per-bar automations.
  - `{HARMONY}`: chord-voice azimuth spreading (equiangular triplet vs. mono-phantom blend).
  - `{TEXTURE}`: angular width, distance, motion speed, and per-voice reverb-send level.
- **Mapping Flow**:
  1. Compose and fill the UnitMatrix; validate zero-drift; export MIDI via the musicom engine (symbolic layer).
  2. Render each voice mono through its assigned synthesis engine (SP-029/SP-016/SP-010/…) into a per-voice buffer.
  3. VBAP-pan each mono buffer along its cell-derived `az/el/d` trajectory into the loudspeaker channels (constant-power gains, per-block vectorized).
  4. Sum channels; apply distance attenuation and per-speaker delay; fold down to binaural headphones via per-speaker HRTFs (SP-021) or decode (SP-034); export stereo/multichannel.

### **Pitfalls**
1. **Degenerate triangles (collinear/coplanar speakers)** → $\det L_{123} \approx 0$ → the inverse blows up (NaN/huge gains). Fix: at mesh build, discard simplices with $|\det L|$ below a threshold (e.g. $10^{-9}$); fall back to the nearest non-degenerate triangle.
2. **Clicks when crossing a triangle edge** — the *active speaker set* changes abruptly at an edge even though the gains are continuous. Fix: equal-power crossfade across the shared edge over a short window, or Pulkki's continuous mesh interpolation; keep LFO/pan rates below the zipper limit and smooth trajectory keyframes.
3. **Normalization confusion (constant-amplitude vs constant-power)** — using $\sum g_i = 1$ instead of $\sum g_i^2 = 1$ bumps loudness at center (phantom-image loudness error). Fix: always apply the $\|\mathbf{g}\|$ normalization; reserve constant-amplitude for intentional near-field level behavior.
4. **Phantom-source instability away from sweet spot** — amplitude-only panning localizes well only near the array center; off-center listeners hear the nearest speaker dominate. Fix: keep the listening area small for critical material, or add distance gain compensation and per-speaker delay alignment; for headphone targets always fold through HRTFs (SP-021).
5. **No elevation without high/top speakers** — a horizontal-only ring cannot carry a source above the plane (the 2D base is rank-deficient in $z$). Fix: hybrid panning with virtual-loudspeaker pairs and top speakers, as in the "hybrid panning" section.
6. **Front–back confusion from gains alone** — equal gains to symmetrically placed front/rear speakers are indistinguishable without timbral/ITD cues. Fix: add HRTF convolution, air-absorption filtering, and distance reverb-send for depth.
7. **Per-sample Python triangle search too slow for many sources** — a naive loop re-tests every triangle every sample. Fix: precompute per-triangle inverse matrices, cache the current triangle per source and only re-test on exit, vectorize trajectory blocks, and JIT/web the per-sample loop.

### **Comparison With Related Methods**
| Method | Spatial model | Speaker dependency | Per-source cost | Sweet spot | Channels |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Binaural HRTF (SP-021) | Per-ear filters (ITD/ILD) | Headphones (2 ch) | 1 convolution pair | Single (head) | 2 |
| HOA (SP-034) | Scene (spherical harmonics) | Any (decode at render) | $O(K)$ | Wide | $(N{+}1)^2$ |
| WFS (SP-043) | Physical wavefront | Dense line/ring array | Convolution per speaker | Wide | $L_s$ |
| **VBAP (SP-053)** | **Object (vector basis)** | **Arbitrary discrete array** | **$O(1)$ gains** | **Center** | **$L_s$** |

- Pulkki, V. (2000). "Generic Panning Tools for MAX/MSP." *Proceedings of the International Computer Music Conference (ICMC)*, Berlin.
- Pulkki, V. (2001). "Localization of Amplitude-Panned Virtual Sources II: Two- and Three-Dimensional Panning." *Journal of the Audio Engineering Society* 49(9), pp. 753–767.
- Pulkki, V., and Karjalainen, M. (2015). *Communication Acoustics: An Introduction to Speech, Audio and Psychoacoustics.* Wiley.
