# Dattorro Plate Reverb (DPR) (Method SP-071)

### Source
The canonical algorithm is **Jon Dattorro (1997), "Effect Design, Part 1: Reverberator and Other Filters," *Journal of the Audio Engineering Society* 45(9), 660–684** — the paper that introduced the now-ubiquitous "figure-8" plate-reverberation topology, with its companion parts **"Effect Design, Part 2: Delay-Line Modulation and Chorus" (JAES 45(10), 764–788)** and **"Effect Design, Part 3: Oscillators and LFOs" (JAES 51(3), 2002)**. The topology itself descends from **Schroeder's (1961/1962) parallel-comb + series-allpass reverberator** and **Griesinger's late-1970s Lexicon 224 plate class**, which Dattorro credits as the direct ancestor ("simplified plate-class reverberation topology in the style of Griesinger"). It models the **EMT 140 physical plate** — the gold-foil steel plate whose bending waves are injected by a transducer and tapped at multiple contact points — but implements the *percept*, not the physics: instantaneous high-density reflections, a smooth exponential decay envelope, and phase-randomized recirculation. The DPR name and coefficient sets are the de-facto standard, re-implemented in countless open-source projects (e.g. the Valley Audio "Plateau" VCV Rack module) and every serious reverb tutorial. It is the plate-class member of the Musicom reverb family — filling the gap between **SP-009** (convolutive room IR, realistic early reflections but fixed), **SP-032** (FDN, parametric but abstract/colorless) and **SP-058** (dispersive spring reverb, metallic "boing").

### Layer
**Absolute** — sound production (post-processing / DSP). DPR consumes an already-rendered mono or stereo audio buffer (from any synthesis engine: SP-001 FluidSynth, SP-029 subtractive, SP-039 additive, or raw VST stems) and emits a reverberated audio signal. It emits no MIDI (`concrete`) and designs no pitch pools (`abstract`). Candidate code path: `sound/effects/dattorro_plate.py` (sibling to `room_reverb.py`, `reverb.py`, `fdn_reverb`*, `shimmer_reverb.py`); the existing `sound/effects/reverb.py` (Schroeder/Moorer) and `sound/effects/room_reverb.py` (comb+allpass) are its simpler ancestors, and DPR is the natural next member of that family.

### Description
Dattorro Plate Reverb is an **algorithmic plate reverberator** built from a cascade of **four input all-pass diffusers** followed by a **recirculating "tank"** — two delay-line loops (left and right) whose input/output all-pass diffusers are cross-coupled into a global **figure-eight** feedback path. The four input all-pass diffusers (a lattice topology, each an up-sampled first-order all-pass) decorrelate the incoming signal before it enters the tank, turning even a sharp transient into phase-randomized material so the recirculation does not read as a cyclic event. The tank itself holds the signal in a global feedback loop whose two low-pass "damping" filters roll off high frequencies with each pass — the perceptual signature of a plate, where high frequencies decay faster than lows. Seven output taps (with a fixed ±0.6 weighting pattern) are drawn from various points inside the tank to synthesize a wide stereo image from a *monophonic* tank input. The whole network runs at the paper's nominal **29 761 Hz** sample rate with delays specified in that clock; implementations scale every delay by `f_s / 29761` to run at the host rate. Two slow LFOs (≈0.1–0.18 Hz, peak excursion 16 samples) modulate the four tank all-pass delay lines to break up audible modes ("the picket-fence effect") — the closest a static network gets to the ever-shifting modal density of a real plate. Key knobs: **predelay**, **bandwidth** (input low-pass), **decay** (reverb time), **decay diffusion 1/2** (tail density and decorrelation), **input diffusion 1/2**, and **damping** (HF decay within the tank).

### Technical Mechanics

**1. All-pass lattice diffuser (the atomic building block).** Each of the eight diffusers is a two-multiplier lattice whose transfer function is all-pass when its two coefficients are identical (`g`):

$$y[n] = -g\,x[n] + x[n-M] + g\,y[n-M] \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad H(z)=\frac{-g + z^{-M}}{1 - g\,z^{-M}}$$

For `g=0` the filter is a pure delay; for `|g|→1` the impulse response becomes a long, exponentially-decaying sequence of up-sampled first-order-allpass responses — i.e. it *spreads* a click into a diffuse burst while leaving the magnitude spectrum untouched. Negative `g` flips the impulse-response sign each period (the `(-1)^{n-M}` character change Dattorro exploits in the "decay diffusion 1" pair).

**2. Input stage.** Mono sum → predelay `z^{-P}` → one-pole low-pass (bandwidth coefficient `bw=0.9995`, i.e. cutoff ≈ 2 kHz at 29 761 Hz) → four series input all-pass diffusers (`g=0.75`, `0.75`, `0.625`, `0.625`). The all-pass cascade decorrelates the signal before it feeds the tank.

**3. Tank (figure-eight).** Two identical halves (left/right). Each half: input sum → decay-diffusion all-pass 1 (`g=-0.70`, delay 672) → delay line `D1` (4453 left / 4217 right) → one-pole low-pass damping filter (`damping=0.0005` → `y[n]=(1-d)y[n]+d\,y[n-1]`, `d≈0.9995`, cutoff ≈ 2 kHz) → decay-diffusion all-pass 2 (`g=0.50` = `decay+0.15`, delay 1800 left / 2656 right) → delay line `D2` (3720 left / 3163 right). Then the **cross-coupling** that closes the figure-eight:

$$\text{leftSum} = \text{decay}\cdot D2_R[n], \qquad \text{rightSum} = \text{decay}\cdot D2_L[n]$$

so each half's output feeds the *opposite* half's input through the single **decay** coefficient (`decay=0.5` default). This global recirculation is what holds the tail; the delay lengths `{4453, 3720, 4217, 3163}` (incommensurate, all ≈ 100–150 ms) plus the four modulated all-pass delays are what make the echo density climb fast enough to read as a smooth decay rather than a loop.

**4. Output taps.** From the paper's Table 2 (all-wet, synthetic stereo from a mono tank):

$$Y_L = 0.6\,(t_{1,L}+t_{2,L}-t_{3,L}+t_{4,L}-t_{5,L}-t_{6,L}-t_{7,L}), \qquad
Y_R = 0.6\,(t_{1,R}+t_{2,R}-t_{3,R}+t_{4,R}-t_{5,R}-t_{6,R}-t_{7,R})$$

with the tap locations (at 29 761 Hz; scaled by `f_s/29761` for other rates) drawn from the two delay lines and the four tank all-passes. The ± signs and interleaved delay/tap positions decorrelate left from right — a synthetic stereo image from a mono reverberator, a defining plate trait.

**5. Delay-line modulation.** The two indicated tank taps (nodes 24 and 48 in Dattorro's Fig. 1; in the Plateau re-implementation, all four tank all-pass delay lines) are modulated by slow LFOs (0.1–0.18 Hz, excursions up to ±16 samples) using linear or all-pass fractional-delay interpolation. This injects a slow, imperceptible pitch undulation that smears the static comb modes of the tank — turning "picket-fence" resonances into a continuously shifting modal field.

**6. Magnitude truncation.** Dattorro's implementation detail (not in the transfer functions): recursive lattices produce low-level zero-input limit-cycle tones after the input stops; **magnitude truncation** (truncation toward zero) of the double-precision intermediate written to delay memory drives the tail to absolute digital silence — a 12–24 dB noise-floor improvement at the cost of ≤6 dB extra THD+N on steady tones. In a float32/float64 NumPy implementation the limit-cycle issue is moot, but the DC-block of input and output (20 Hz, as in Plateau) is retained to keep the one-pole filters from accumulating DC.

**7. Computational load.** Each sample: 4 input all-passes + 4 tank all-passes + 4 delay-line reads/writes + 3 one-pole filters + 14 output-tap reads. Roughly **11 multiplies and ~25 delay-line reads per sample** for full stereo — trivial for offline rendering in NumPy and real-time-safe. Deterministic per seed once the LFO phases and delay states are initialized; the LFO modulation is the only time-varying component and it is fully determined by its (seedable) initial phase.

### Musical Elements Framework

| Element | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **PITCH** | unaffected — DPR is an LTI (modulo the slow LFO) post-processor: it adds no harmonic content, only a dense tail. The LFO modulation imparts a sub-1 Hz pitch undulation (≤ a few cents) that is perceptually inaudible as vibrato but essential to smearing tank modes |
| **RHYTHM** | predelay (`P`, 0–~120 ms) sets the gap between dry attack and first reflection burst — a rhythmic "air" control that can be tuned to a subdivision; the echo-density ramp of the figure-eight (~ms to tens of ms) is the "attack" of the space; decay coefficient sets how long each onset rings |
| **HARMONY** | none directly; but the damping low-pass and input bandwidth filter *re-tune* the perceived brightness of sustained harmony — low damping = bright, metallic plate (long ring on high strings/cymbals); high damping = dark, warm plate. The tank's ~2000 Hz cutoff means the tail carries fundamentals + low partials, subtly reinforcing the low register of a chord |
| **STRUCTURE** | per-section parameter automation = macro-form: verse = short decay / low predelay (tight, intimate); chorus = long decay / high diffusion (open, wide); bridge = freeze (decay→1.0) or long predelay; section joins = parameter crossfade (the reverb analogue of SP-041 wavetable morphing). The decay coefficient is the single most musically decisive knob |
| **TEXTURE** | the plate's defining feature: instantaneous high-density reflections + smooth exponential decay with phase-randomized recirculation. Diffusion knobs set how "smeared" vs "discrete" the tail reads; damping sets dark/bright; output tap weights set stereo width. Dense polyphonic UnitMatrix textures benefit from the plate's fast reflection build-up (no gap), which is exactly why plates flatter vocals/drums/strings |

### UnitMatrix Integration

- **Rows (Voices)**: two modes. **(a) Bus mode** — all rendered voices summed to mono (or stereo) and passed through one DPR instance: the classic "mix-bus plate" that glues the whole mix into one cohesive space (the shared tank couples the voices' tails). **(b) Per-voice mode** — each voice `v` gets its own DPR with independent decay/damping/predelay, rendered to a mono buffer then summed or spatialized (SP-021/034/043): bright short-decay plate on percussion, long dark plate on pads, no reverb on bass. Each row's wet/dry mix is a per-voice send level.
- **Columns (Sections)** = `{STRUCTURE}` = `(predelay, bandwidth, decay, diffusion1, diffusion2, damping, freeze)` per section. A section boundary swaps the parameter vector; a continuous crossfade across a join = smooth space morph (verse's tight room → chorus's cathedral). `freeze=True` holds decay at 1.0 for an infinite-sustain section (a drone/outro effect).
- **Cells (MusicUnit)** = `{RHYTHM}` → predelay can be locked to a note subdivision; `{TEXTURE}` → diffusion/damping per cell (e.g. brighter plate for accented cells); `{HARMONY}` → damping low-pass gently re-voices sustained cells. DPR is a *render-stage* transform: the `MusicUnit` grid is composed and validated (zero-drift gate) exactly as usual, then `produce()` runs each voice buffer through DPR after synthesis and before the final EQ/DRC/master chain.
- **Flow**: `compose` (UnitMatrix MIDI) → `produce(method="SP-071")` → per-voice (or bus) DPR render → sum voices → post-FX (SP-007 EQ, SP-008 DRC) → export WAV/OGG. Pairs with SP-009 (convolutive IR for realistic early reflections, DPR for the dense plate tail), SP-032 (FDN as the colorless parametric alternative), and SP-058 (spring reverb for a metallic, non-plate character). Per the Method Hybridization rule, a plate adds continuous depth to *any* sparse-rhythm source — it is a canonical continuous-fill *space*, not a rhythmic generator, so pair it with 011/032-driven material to smooth staccato textures.

### Pitfalls
1. **Sample-rate coupling** — every delay and tap coordinate is specified at 29 761 Hz. Running the raw constants at 44.1/48 kHz shrinks the tank (~1.5×) and shifts the perceived size/pitch of the tail. Fix: scale *all* delays by `f_s / 29761` (Dattorro's own scaling rule; Plateau's `dattorroScale()`); never copy the raw sample counts.
2. **All-pass lattice clips internally** — the two-multiplier lattice tends to clip prematurely at internal nodes for full-scale input at some frequencies (Dattorro's explicit warning). Fix: run the diffusers in float64 with generous headroom, apply an input gain ~0.5 (Dattorro's mono sum uses 0.5× per channel), and place the DC-block/HPF *before* the tank so a DC offset never accumulates through the feedback loop.
3. **"Picket-fence" modes without modulation** — a static tank exhibits audible resonant comb modes (audible "ringing" on drum material). Fix: modulate the tank all-pass delays with the slow LFOs (0.1–0.18 Hz, ±8–16 samples); without this the decay reads as a fixed filter bank, not a plate.
4. **Decay-coefficient interaction with diffusion** — `decay diffusion 2 = decay + 0.15` must stay inside [0.25, 0.50]; letting it track `decay` naively pushes the all-pass coefficient toward 1.0 (buzzing, instability risk when `g` → 1.0). Fix: clamp as the paper specifies (floor 0.25, ceiling 0.50) and keep `|g| < 1.0` strictly (0.9999999 max).
5. **HF damping is a *coefficient*, not a cutoff** — `damping=0.0005` is a one-pole coefficient (`d≈0.9995`), and its *high* value means *lower* cutoff; the input-bandwidth coefficient tracks the *opposite* convention (`bw=0.9995` = full bandwidth). Confusing the two conventions inverts the tone control. Fix: document each knob's convention and default to the paper's table values.
6. **Freeze diverges without decay reset** — setting `decay=1.0` for a freeze hold makes the tank lossless and any DC or numerical residue circulates forever, growing to full-scale. Fix: DC-block input and output (20 Hz), use magnitude-truncation semantics (or periodic tiny decay) so the frozen tail stays bounded, and crossfade the freeze in over ~100 ms (Plateau's `_fade`) to avoid a discontinuity click.
7. **Stereo collapse on mono sources** — DPR synthesizes stereo from a mono tank, but feeding it a *mono-summed* input discards the input's own stereo image. Fix: keep the input stereo path (or sum-then-spread deliberately); if a true stereo tail is needed, run two slightly-detuned DPR instances (L/R) or pair with SP-021/034 spatialization on the wet return.

### Comparison With Related Methods

| Method | Space model | Early reflections | Tail synthesis | HF damping | Cost/sample | Character |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SP-009 Convolutive | measured IR | real (in IR) | IR tail | in IR | O(L) convolution | realistic, fixed |
| SP-032 FDN | unitary feedback net | synthetic | matrix diffusion | per-line filter | O(N) | parametric, colorless |
| SP-058 DWSR | spring waveguide | n/a (metallic) | dispersive all-pass chain | one-pole | O(1) | "boing"/drip |
| room_reverb.py | image-source taps | tapped delay | comb+allpass | tilt | O(1) | small-room |
| **SP-071 DPR** | **figure-eight plate tank** | **4 input all-passes** | **cross-coupled tank + 7 taps** | **in-loop one-pole** | **O(1)** | **dense, warm plate** |

# Hidden Markov Model Latent-State Composition (HMM-C) (Method 086)

### Source
The Hidden Markov Model was formalized by **Leonard E. Baum & Ted Petrie (1966), "Statistical Inference for Probabilistic Functions of Finite State Markov Chains," *Annals of Mathematical Statistics* 37(6), 1554–1563**, and the three canonical algorithms — the **forward–backward** recursion, the **Baum–Welch** (EM) parameter re-estimation, and the **Viterbi** decoding path — were consolidated by **Lawrence R. Rabiner (1989), "A Tutorial on Hidden Markov Models and Selected Applications in Speech Recognition," *Proceedings of the IEEE* 77(2), 257–286**, the paper that made HMMs the default sequential-latent-state model in signal processing. The musical lineage is equally direct: **Ponsford, Wiggins & Mellish (1999), "Statistical Learning of Harmonic Movement," *Journal of New Music Research* 28(2), 150–177**, learned harmonic-progression HMMs from Bach chorales; **Christopher Raphael (2002), "A Hybrid Graphical Model for Rhythmic Parsing," *Artificial Intelligence* 137(1–2), 217–238**, used a hidden-state graphical model for score-following and rhythm; **Sheh & Ellis (2003), "Chord Segmentation and Recognition Using EM-Trained Hidden Markov Models," *ISMIR***, made HMM chord recognition a standard; and **Allan & Williams (2005), "Harmonising Chorales by Probabilistic Inference," *NeurIPS 17***, used an HMM over hidden harmonic states to harmonize melodies. HMM-C inverts this *analysis/recognition* tool into a *generator*: the hidden chain is the composition plan, and the emissions are the sounding music.

### Layer
**concrete** — emits actual `MusicEvent`s (pitch, onset, velocity) into UnitMatrix cells by sampling (or Viterbi-decoding) an emission from a hidden state at each step; feeds `generators/`. The hidden-state sequence itself is an abstract-layer object (a tension/function curve over HOME/LIFT/TENSE/TURN that could seed `rules/subset_network.py` ABS-001/002), but as documented the method realizes events, so it is **concrete**. Candidate code path: `generators/hmm_composition.py`.

### Description
A Hidden Markov Model is a doubly stochastic process: a **hidden** first-order Markov chain over discrete states $q_t \in \{1..S\}$ that is never observed directly, and a **visible** emission $o_t$ drawn at each step from a state-conditioned distribution. The model is the tuple $\lambda = (A, B, \pi)$:

- $\pi_i = P(q_1 = i)$ — the initial-state distribution (where the piece starts);
- $A_{ij} = P(q_{t+1} = j \mid q_t = i)$ — the **transition matrix**, the harmonic/structural grammar;
- $B_i(o) = P(o_t = o \mid q_t = i)$ — the **emission matrix**, the surface vocabulary of each state.

Composition is the *generative direction* of HMM inference. Three modes:

1. **Unconditional sampling**: draw $q_1 \sim \pi$, then alternately $q_{t+1} \sim A_{q_t,\cdot}$ and $o_t \sim B_{q_t}$ — a free stochastic walk whose macro-structure is governed entirely by the transition grammar (self-loops = phrase holds, off-diagonal mass = modulation/progression).
2. **Viterbi-forced composition**: fix the emission sequence (a target melody/skeleton, or an abstract form template) and decode the single most probable hidden path $\hat q = \arg\max_q P(q \mid o, \lambda)$ — the optimal "harmonic interpretation" of the surface. This is re-harmonization as generation: new music = old surface + decoded structure.
3. **Section-conditioned composition (per-column state priors)**: force $q_t$ into a chosen subset during section $s$ (e.g. states $\{1,2\}$ for verse, $\{3\}$ for chorus). This couples the HMM to the UnitMatrix's section columns, so the hidden chain *is* the macro-form.

Training (Baum–Welch) learns $A$ and $B$ from a corpus of target-style excerpts: the learned transition matrix encodes the style's harmonic grammar (probable HOME→LIFT→TENSE→TURN movements), and the learned emissions encode its melodic/rhythmic vocabulary. States then admit a musically meaningful interpretation: with a suitably restricted state space, the hidden states align with tonal function (HOME/LIFT/TENSE/TURN), chord regions, or structural sections.

### Technical Mechanics

**The three algorithms** (all standard; complexity below for $T$ time steps, $S$ states, $V$ emission symbols):

1. **Forward–backward** — computes $\alpha_t(i) = P(o_{1:t}, q_t = i)$ and $\beta_t(i) = P(o_{t+1:T} \mid q_t = i)$ by the recurrences

$$\alpha_t(j) = \left[\sum_i \alpha_{t-1}(i) A_{ij}\right] B_j(o_t), \qquad \beta_t(i) = \sum_j A_{ij} B_j(o_{t+1}) \beta_{t+1}(j),$$

so $P(O \mid \lambda) = \sum_i \alpha_T(i)$. This is the basis of all HMM inference.

2. **Baum–Welch (EM)** — re-estimates the parameters by counting the expected transitions/emissions under the forward–backward posterior:

$$\gamma_t(i) = \frac{\alpha_t(i)\beta_t(i)}{P(O\mid\lambda)}, \qquad
\xi_t(i,j) = \frac{\alpha_t(i) A_{ij} B_j(o_{t+1}) \beta_{t+1}(j)}{P(O\mid\lambda)},$$

$$A_{ij} \leftarrow \frac{\sum_t \xi_t(i,j)}{\sum_t \gamma_t(i)}, \qquad
B_i(k) \leftarrow \frac{\sum_{t:\,o_t=k} \gamma_t(i)}{\sum_t \gamma_t(i)}, \qquad
\pi_i \leftarrow \gamma_1(i).$$

Iterated to convergence, this is maximum-likelihood training of $A$ and $B$ from a corpus. **Complexity** $\mathcal{O}(I \cdot T \cdot S^2)$ for $I$ iterations.

3. **Viterbi decoding** — the dynamic-programming max-path:

$$\delta_t(j) = \max_i \left[ \delta_{t-1}(i) A_{ij} \right] B_j(o_t),$$

with backpointers recovered to yield $\hat q$. This finds the single best hidden-state explanation of an observation sequence. **Complexity** $\mathcal{O}(T \cdot S^2 \cdot V)$ when emission evaluation is included.

**Underflow**: $\alpha_t, \beta_t, \delta_t$ decay geometrically in $T$; implement in log-space ($\log\alpha$, $\log\beta$, $\log\delta$) and use the log-sum-exp trick, or rescale at each step. **Tie-breaking determinism**: Baum–Welch is non-convex (local optima) — seed the RNG and fix iteration count for the zero-drift gate; Viterbi ties broken by lowest state index for reproducibility.

### Musical Elements Framework

| Element | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **PITCH** | emission distribution $B_i$ over pitch classes / scale degrees per hidden state. A state's emission = its melodic vocabulary: HOME emits chord tones of the tonic with high probability, TENSE emits chromatic/leading-tone classes, TURN emits passing tones. Sampling $o_t \sim B_{q_t}$ at each step yields the melody; the same pitch class maps to a register via a state- or section-dependent octave profile |
| **RHYTHM** | two channels: (a) a separate emission symbol stream over rhythmic cells (onset patterns / IOI classes) so each hidden state has a *groove* distribution; (b) the self-loop probability $A_{ii}$ controls dwell time — high $A_{ii}$ = long held notes / sustained state (legato), low $A_{ii}$ = rapid state turnover (busy, sectional). State-holding time is geometrically distributed with mean $1/(1-A_{ii})$, which maps directly to phrase length |
| **HARMONY** | the hidden state *is* the harmonic identity. A well-trained $A$ encodes the functional grammar (HOME→LIFT→TENSE→TURN arcs); the *decoded* or *forced* state path is the chord progression. $B_i$'s emission mass over pitch classes = the chord/scale content of state $i$ (co-occurring pitch classes = a chord voicing). Forcing a state subset per section = harmonic modulation (verse in HOME-region states, bridge in LIFT/TURN-region states) |
| **STRUCTURE** | the state path = macro-form. With $S$ states interpreted as sections/functions, the transition matrix's macro-block structure (near-block-diagonal $A$ with sparse off-block leaks) yields verse–chorus/rondo form; a single recurrent component = through-composed flow. Viterbi over a *form template* (a designed emission skeleton) fixes the structural plan deterministically; unconditional sampling lets it emerge from $A$ |
| **TEXTURE** | state-conditioned emission multiplicity: a state whose emission distributes mass over *several simultaneous* symbols (a chord cell, a drum pattern) is a dense state; one with a sparse single-note emission is thin. The dwell time (self-loop) × multiplicity sets per-cell density. A low-entropy $B_i$ (peaked) = repetitive/ostinato texture; high-entropy $B_i$ = varied/ornamental texture |

### UnitMatrix Integration (Voices & Sections)
- **Rows (Voices)** = parallel hidden chains, either **(a) coupled**: one hidden state chain $q_t$ shared by all voices, each voice drawing its own emission from the *same* state (vertical coherence — a state emits a chord voicing split across voices), or **(b) independent per-voice chains** with a coupling emission (voice $v$ emits from $B^{(v)}$ conditioned on the shared state → independence + consonance). A third mode couples voices via a *product* emission over a joint pitch-class vector (the chord), which is the HMM analogue of 064 MRFCC's vertical clique potentials.
- **Columns (Sections)** = forced state subsets. Each section records `(allowed_states, initial_state_prior, dwell_bias)`. Intro = states with high self-loop (sustained HOME); verse = HOME/LIFT region; chorus = maximal-multiplicity dense states; bridge = TENSE/TURN states (off-diagonal $A$ mass = novelty); outro = decay to a single terminal state (cadence on finalis).
- **Cells (MusicUnit)** = `{PITCH}` = sampled emission pitch class (+ octave profile); `{RHYTHM}` = emission rhythmic cell + onset from dwell-time; `{HARMONY}` = hidden state → function label (HOME/LIFT/TENSE/TURN by state index); `{TEXTURE}` = emission entropy + multiplicity → accent/density. Deterministic per seed (seeded RNG + fixed Baum–Welch iterations + fixed tie-break) → zero-drift gate holds; hand to `UnitMatrixComposer` per AGENTS.md.
- **Flow**: `train(corpus, S, seed)` (or hand-set $A,B,\pi$) → `force_sections(section_specs)` → `sample_path()` / `viterbi_force(target)` → decode $(q_t, o_t)$ to `create_note_unit`/`create_chord_unit` cells → `composer.validate()` must be True before `to_midi`.

### Pitfalls
1. **Log-underflow** — raw $\alpha_t/\beta_t/\delta_t$ underflow to 0 for $T \gtrsim 100$ at machine precision. Fix: implement the three recursions entirely in log-space (log-sum-exp), the standard Rabiner scaling alternative being the only other safe choice.
2. **State-count mismatch** — too few states merges distinct functions (HOME and LIFT collapse into one), too many splits a single function into near-duplicate states. Fix: sweep $S$ (e.g. 4–16) and pick the knee of held-out log-likelihood, or pin $S$ to the number of chord functions + sections expected.
3. **Non-convex training drift** — Baum–Welch converges to local optima; different seeds → different $A,B$ → different "same" composition. Fix: seed RNG + fixed iteration count for determinism; initialize $A$ with a functional prior (self-loops high, HOME→LIFT allowed, no LIFT→HOME reversal) to land in musically sensible optima.
4. **Viterbi tie ambiguity** — equal-scoring hidden paths (degenerate $A$ or uniform $B$) make the decoded structure unstable. Fix: deterministic tie-break (lowest state index), and add a tiny prior or temperature to $A$ to break exact ties.
5. **Sparse/staccato emission hazard** — a per-step sampled emission can produce gap-filled, staccato textures, especially with low self-loop mass. Per the Method Hybridization rule, pair HMM-C with a continuous fill layer (026 DPSM arpeggios, sustained pad, or walking bass) when it is the sole rhythmic generator.
6. **Emission granularity coupling** — $B$ learned at one granularity (pitch class vs chord symbol vs rhythmic cell) cannot be decoded at another. Fix: fix the emission alphabet per element (pitch-class for melody, chord for harmony, IOI-cell for rhythm) and use separate HMM layers or a factored (multi-stream) emission for each element rather than mixing them in one alphabet.
7. **Unseen-emission zero probability** — a corpus-trained $B$ assigns $0$ to tokens absent from training, crashing inference on novel input. Fix: Laplace/floor smoothing ($B_i(o) \leftarrow (c + \delta)/(\cdot)$) so every symbol has positive probability.

### Comparison With Related Methods
| Method | State | Learning | Structure source | Generation |
